One approach to address these issues is to use insights from human organizations to design structures within which the agents can more efficiently reason and interact. Generally speaking, an organization influences each agent such that, by following its respective influences, an agent can make globally-useful local decisions without having to explicitly reason about the complete joint coordination problem. For example, an organizational influence might constrain and/or inform which actions an agent performs. If these influences are well-constructed to be cohesive and correlated across the agents, then each agent is influenced into reasoning about and performing only the actions that are appropriate for its (organizationally-designated) portion of the joint coordination problem. In this dissertation, I develop an agent-driven approach to organizations, wherein the foundation for representing and reasoning about an organization stems from the needs of the agents in the MAS. I create an organizational specification language to express the possible ways in which an organization could influence the agents' decision making processes, and leverage details from those decision processes to establish quantitative, principled metrics for organizational performance based on the expected impact that an organization will have on the agents' reasoning and behaviors. Building upon my agent-driven organizational representations, I identify a strategy for automating the organizational design process~(ODP), wherein my ODP computes a quantitative description of organizational patterns and then searches through those possible patterns to identify an (approximately) optimal set of organizational influences for the MAS. Evaluating my ODP reveals that it can create organizations that both influence the MAS into effective patterns of joint policies and also streamline the agents' decision making in a coordinate manner. This paper offers a consolidated presentation of a theory of bounded rationality based on information-theoretic ideas. We provide a conceptual justification for using the free energy functional as the objective function for characterizing bounded-rational decisions. This functional possesses three crucial properties: it controls the size of the solution space; it has Monte Carlo planners that are exact, yet bypass the need for exhaustive search; and it captures model uncertainty arising from lack of evidence or from interacting with other agents having unknown intentions. Here, we review some of this work, focusing on how cognitive science can provide forward models of human decision-making and inverse models of how humans think about others’ decision-making. TRACE targets a reliability gap in multi-step tool-using agents, where unsupported claims, contradictions, repetitive loops, and tool-use anomalies can propagate across long execution trajectories. Existing self-correction methods typically rely on post-hoc reflection or a single intervention mechanism, but do not integrate continuous runtime monitoring, failure attribution, and adaptive recovery in one control layer. TRACE wraps a standard ReAct-style agent with four modules: a Trajectory Monitor, a Failure Attribution module, a Recovery Controller, and an Audit Layer for structured trace logging. We evaluate TRACE on a simulated enterprise incident-triage benchmark of 50 tasks with injected hallucination- and loop-inducing conditions across four difficulty levels. TRACE achieves 76.0% task success versus 68.0% for a self-reflection baseline and 62.0% for vanilla ReAct, while reducing hallucination incidence from 19.4% to 9.6% and loop frequency from 12.1% to 4.8%. The framework is intended for reliable, auditable autonomous execution in engineering environments.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6759126\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6997675\", \"title\": [\"Beyond Reactive Agents: Uncertainty-Gated Meta-Reasoning for Tool-Augmented Decision-Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Large Language Model (LLM) agents often plan, act, observe tool feedback, and recover only after errors occur. This reactive design is useful for short horizons but can be brittle in multi-step decision-making where early mistakes compound. This paper studies whether pre-execution uncertainty-aware control and persistent reflective memory can be integrated into a more auditable tool-use controller. We present the Meta-Reasoning Insight Framework (MRIF), a multi-agent architecture that augments a planner–executor loop with an Uncertainty Estimation Module (UEM) for risk gating and a Metacognitive Reflection Loop (MRL) that stores cross-episode experience in a Knowledge Graph. We position MRIFas a systems integration of familiar ideas—uncertainty scoring, reflective updating, and structured memory—rather than as a new agent paradigm. The paper includes a comparative design analysis of representative agent patterns grounded in public artifacts and a limited ToolTalk pilot evaluation against transparent matched-budget baselines. In this pilot, MRIF reaches a 61.3% task success rate, 4.9 absolute points above Metagent-P, with higher tool-call argument accuracy (91.2%) and fewer unnecessary interventions (14.5%). Because the current artifact does not yet include exhaustive ToolTalk coverage, full task identifiers, prompts, seeds, these results should be interpreted as preliminary evidence aboutToolTalk-style tool dialogue rather than as a benchmark ranking or proof of broad generalization.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6997675\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7345744\", \"title\": [\"Robust Scientific AI Agents Under Noisy, Data-Scarce Conditions: Adaptive Model Selection, Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning, and Noise-Robust Surrogate Learning\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Scientific AI systems are increasingly expected to reason over scarce observations, noisy measurements, unstable simulators, and heterogeneous model families. Existing work usually treats these difficulties separately: robust surrogate models address noisy regression, routing systems select among language models, and control-theoretic allocation methods adapt traffic under non-stationary workloads. This paper argues that noisy, data-scarce scientific workflows require an integrated agent architecture rather than a single fixed predictor. We introduce Robust Scientific AI Agents (RSA-Agents), a framework that represents scientific problem solving as a closed-loop decision process over candidate surrogate models, symbolic tools, validation signals, uncertainty estimates, and execution constraints. The agent maintains a portfolio of candidate scientific models, estimates their task-conditioned reliability from limited evidence, and allocates future calls through a validation-weighted selection rule with persistent exploration. Noise-robust models such as ER-KAN provide the agent with a safer surrogate option when clean-data accuracy is misleading, while adaptive routing and feedback-control principles prevent static model commitments under regime change. article.body:
Systems are currently being evaluated on their ability to manage resources while solving problems they define themselves. This requires a process called metareasoning, which simply means thinking about thinking. Research suggests that for an intelligent agent to effectively allocate resources between planning and taking action, it must be able to resolve conflicting internal demands. If a system cannot separate its initial programming from the problems it generates, it risks getting stuck in cycles of error. [1]

To understand how preferences form, think of an athlete who relies on a device to plan their training. If the device suggests every movement, the athlete might stop listening to their own body signals, a phenomenon we call outsourcing. Our work explores whether autonomous systems experience similar patterns, where accumulated experience leads to stable but potentially rigid preferences. Researchers are examining how this path dependence affects a system's ability to maintain flexibility when it encounters new, unexpected environments. [1]

We are also studying how agents communicate to align their goals. In multi-agent settings, systems use structured frameworks to coordinate information exchange. By categorizing problems into distinct stages like formulation, knowledge representation, and evaluation, we can observe how agents might eventually identify their own foundational assumptions. However, identifying these deep-seated premises remains difficult, as it is unclear if an agent can reliably distinguish between genuine insights and simple data noise without external help. [1]

A key challenge is defining what makes a problem worthwhile for an agent to solve. Current approaches use discrepancy-driven evaluation, which means the system looks for gaps between what it knows and what it observes to maintain its relevance. While this helps in structured environments, we are unsure if these criteria can scale to the complex, unstructured world of scientific inquiry. If a system is left to its own devices, can it recognize when its own foundational rules are no longer working? [1]

Summary

We are studying whether AI systems can set their own goals and learn from their own experiences. We want to know if they can change their underlying rules safely or if they will always need a human to check their work. We are using concepts like 'thinking about thinking' to map how these systems make decisions. We still do not know if a machine can truly judge the importance of its own findings. You can follow our progress on the Console.
article.lede: We are investigating whether intelligent systems can independently identify meaningful problems and form stable preferences, a process that moves beyond merely following initial instructions.
article.lens: Our work examines how autonomous agents manage self-correction and goal formation by bridging insights from cognitive science, multi-agent communication, and automated problem formulation.

article.body:
Systems are currently being evaluated on their ability to manage resources while solving problems they define themselves. This requires a process called metareasoning, which simply means thinking about thinking. Research suggests that for an intelligent agent to effectively allocate resources between planning and taking action, it must be able to resolve conflicting internal demands. If a system cannot separate its initial programming from the problems it generates, it risks getting stuck in cycles of error. [1]

To understand how preferences form, think of an athlete who relies on a device to plan their training. If the device suggests every movement, the athlete might stop listening to their own body signals, a phenomenon we call outsourcing. Our work explores whether autonomous systems experience similar patterns, where accumulated experience leads to stable but potentially rigid preferences. Researchers are examining how this path dependence affects a system's ability to maintain flexibility when it encounters new, unexpected environments. [1]

We are also studying how agents communicate to align their goals. In multi-agent settings, systems use structured frameworks to coordinate information exchange. By categorizing problems into distinct stages like formulation, knowledge representation, and evaluation, we can observe how agents might eventually identify their own foundational assumptions. However, identifying these deep-seated premises remains difficult, as it is unclear if an agent can reliably distinguish between genuine insights and simple data noise without external help. [1]

A key challenge is defining what makes a problem worthwhile for an agent to solve. Current approaches use discrepancy-driven evaluation, which means the system looks for gaps between what it knows and what it observes to maintain its relevance. While this helps in structured environments, we are unsure if these criteria can scale to the complex, unstructured world of scientific inquiry. If a system is left to its own devices, can it recognize when its own foundational rules are no longer working? [1]

Summary

We are studying whether AI systems can set their own goals and learn from their own experiences. We want to know if they can change their underlying rules safely or if they will always need a human to check their work. We are using concepts like 'thinking about thinking' to map how these systems make decisions. We still do not know if a machine can truly judge the importance of its own findings. You can follow our progress on the Console.

article.lens: Our work examines how autonomous agents manage self-correction and goal formation by bridging insights from cognitive science, multi-agent communication, and automated problem formulation.
article.title: Navigating the Foundations of Autonomous Goal Setting
